books.section: Topic 6.6 The Rise of Industrial Capitalism
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904)

options.text: Its profits depended entirely on a single year's sales
options.misconception: Tarbell gives five years of dividends, not one year's sales.

options.text: Its profits were steady, protected by an ample reserve fund
Its profits were spent at once on new oil wells
options.misconception: The passage says nothing about spending profits on new wells.

options.text: Its profits fell every year as rivals grew
options.misconception: Tarbell counts steady dividends over five years, not falling profits.

rationales.A: Tarbell counts dividends averaging about $45 million a year for five years, not a single year's sales.
rationales.B: Tarbell says the company “allows an annual average of 5.77 per cent. for deficit, and it carries always an ample reserve fund” — the profits were steady and guarded, not a one-year windfall.
rationales.C: The passage never says what the profits were spent on; it counts them and describes the reserve.
rationales.D: Five years of steady dividends averaging about $45 million a year is the opposite of falling profits.
rationales.general:
Read the end of the passage, past the big numbers.
1. Tarbell counts enormous profits: about $45 million a year in dividends.
2. Then she adds that the company allows 5.77 percent for deficit each year.
3. And it “carries always an ample reserve fund.”
4. A company that plans for deficits and keeps a reserve expects its profits to last.
Remember: a reserve fund is a sign of steady profits, not shaky ones.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)
stem: What does Tarbell suggest about how secure Standard Oil's profits were?

stimulus.source_note: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company, Vol. 2, Chapter 18 (1904), public domain.
stimulus.text: “The profits of the present Standard Oil Company are enormous. For five years the dividends have been averaging about forty-five million dollars a year, or nearly fifty per cent. on its capitalisation, a sum which capitalised at five per cent. would give $900,000,000. Of course this is not all that the combination makes in a year. It allows an annual average of 5.77 per cent. for deficit, and it carries always an ample reserve fund.”
